newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Labour govt would repeal ECA regardless - Clark.
newsitem.headline: NZ Labour govt would repeal ECA regardless - Clark.

text.p: TIMARU, Sept 25 - A Labour-led government would introduce legislation to repeal the Employment Contracts Act regardless of whether it could get agreement from its coalition partners for the change, leader Helen Clark said on Wednesday.
NZPA reported Clark saying that after introducing the legislation, Labour would ask the public to lobby parties holding the balance of power to support the changes.
"That is the way the political system is going to work," Clark told a meeting in Timaru.
She made the comments after being asked whether she would trade off Labour's policy of repealing the Act in order to get a coalition agreement.
New Zealand First, a prospective coalition partner, favours less radical change to the Act.
"I'll get the legislation in," Clark said. "Then I need your support to lobby to get a good piece of legislation out of the select committee."
She later told reporters the move would force NZ First to take a position on the extent of changes it wanted to the Act.
"NZ First policy is fluid...That's why I stress the importance of getting legislation out there on the table."
"They can look at that and see (if) that's the sort of change they were thinking about."
The move would clear the way for coalition negotiations, Clark said. Where agreement could not be reached, parties should be free to introduce legislation, she said.
Earlier, Clark defended Labour's social spending plans, which have been criticised by economics consultancy firm Infometrics.
Speaking at a public meeting in Oamaru, she said Labour would continue to pay back public debt, if not at the "giddy" rate of the National Government.
However, any suggestion that Labour would put the economic recovery at risk was "utter rubbish".
Labour planned to use the fruits of economic growth to provide for sound health and education systems, and to ensure security and better services for older people.
Infometrics, in a report out last night, said Labour's plans to spend more and cut the budget surplus gave it the riskiest fiscal approach of all four major parties.
Clark pitched both of her speeches today at older voters, saying in Oamaru that they would never share the benefits of recovery while National remained in office.
This morning Clark briefly visited the modest grave of former Labour prime minister Norman Kirk, who died in office in 1974.
